source_text:
Poterat inquisitioni tuae sufficere mea breuis ista responsio; sed quae alia moueant, quibus respondendum existimo, parumper adtende. in Machabaeorum libris legimus oblatum pro mortuis sacrificium. sed et si nusquam in scripturis ueteribus omnino legeretur, non parua est uniuersae ecclesiae quae in hac consuetudine claret auctoritas, ubi in precibus sacerdotis quae domino deo ad eius altare funduntur locum suum habet etiam commendatio mortuorum.
Sed utrum aliquid prosit animae mortui locus corporis sui, operosius inquirendum est. ac primum utrum intersit aliquid ad inferendam uel augendam miseriam post hanc uitam spiritibus hominum, si eorum corpora sepulta non fuerint, non secundum opinionem utcumque uulgatam, sed potius secundum religionis nostrae sacras litteras est uidendum. neque enim credendum est, sicut apud Maronem legitur, insepultos nauigando atque transeundo inferno amne prohiberi, quia scilicet nec ripas datur horrendas et rauca fluenta transportare prius, quam sedibus ossa quierunt. quis cor christianum inclinet his poeticis fabulosisque figmentis, cum dominus Iesus, ut inter manus inimicorum, qui eorum corpora in potestate haberent, securi occumberent christiani, nec capillum capitis eorum adserat periturum, exhortans ne timeant eos, qui cum corpus occiderint, amplius non habent quid faciant? unde in primo libro de \'Ciuitate dei\' satis, quantum existimo, sum locutus, ut eorum dentem retunderem, qui barbaricam uastitatem, praecipue quam nuper Roma perpessa est, Christianis temporibus inputando etiam id obiciunt, quod suis illic non subuenerit Christus. quibus cum responsum fuerit animas fidelium pro suae fidei meritis ab illo fuisse susceptas, insultant de cadaueribus insepultis. totum itaque istum de sepultura locum uerbis talibus explicaui.
thought_title: Burial place and the soul's misery
orientation: Augustine is answering Paulinus's question about burial, and now turns to ask whether the place of a body helps or harms the soul of the dead.
pass_a_gloss: My brief answer could have been enough for your inquiry; but pay attention for a little while to the other things that move me, to which I think I must respond. In the books of the Maccabees we read that sacrifice was offered for the dead. But even if it were nowhere at all read in the old scriptures, the authority of the universal church is not small, which is clear in this custom, where in the prayers of the priest which are poured out to the Lord God at his altar the prayerful commending of the dead also has its own place. But whether the place of his body helps the soul of a dead man at all is to be inquired into with more labor. And first, whether it matters at all for bringing in or increasing misery after this life for the spirits of men, if their bodies have not been buried, is to be seen not according to any sort of common opinion, but rather according to the sacred writings of our religion. For it must not be believed, as is read in Maro, that the unburied are prevented from sailing and crossing over the river of the underworld, because of course it is not given to transport them across the dreadful banks and hoarse waters before their bones have rested in their resting places. What Christian heart would incline to these poetic and fabulous fictions, when the Lord Jesus, so that Christians might fall securely into the hands of enemies who would have their bodies in their power, asserts that not a hair of their head will perish, exhorting them not to fear those who, when they have killed the body, do not have anything more that they can do? From this in the first book of the City of God I have spoken enough, as I think, to blunt the tooth of those who, charging the barbarian devastation, especially that which Rome recently suffered, to Christian times, also throw this in, that Christ did not come to the aid of his own there. When it has been answered to them that the souls of the faithful were received by him according to the merits of their faith, they insult about the unburied corpses. And so I have explained this whole topic about burial with such words.

choices.why: Glossary term commendatio rendered as prayerful commending, keeping the liturgical sense of commending the dead to God at the altar.
Glossary term inferi rendered as underworld; here inferno amne is the river of the underworld in the Virgilian context.

choices.english: bones have rested in their resting places
choices.why: Keeps the poetic sense of sedibus as resting places for bones, matching the Virgilian paraphrase.
rejected: bones have settled in their seats
bones have found rest in their abodes

choices.why: Renders litteras as writings, the standard term for Scripture in Augustine.
Keeps the metaphor of blunting the tooth of critics, vivid and literal.

bible_refs.note: ne timeant eos, qui cum corpus occiderint, amplius non habent quid faciant
nec capillum capitis eorum adserat periturum

pass_b_english: That brief answer of mine could have been enough for your question, but pay attention for a moment to the other things that trouble people, which I think need a response. In the books of Maccabees we read that sacrifice was offered for the dead. But even if it were nowhere read in the old Scriptures at all, the authority of the whole church, which shines clearly in this custom, is not small: in the prayers of the priest that are poured out to the Lord God at his altar, the prayerful commending of the dead also has its own place.

But whether the place of a person's body helps the soul of the dead is a question that needs more careful work. First, we must consider—not according to some popular opinion, but rather according to the sacred writings of our religion—whether it matters at all for bringing in or increasing misery after this life for the spirits of human beings if their bodies have not been buried. For we must not believe, as is read in Virgil, that the unburied are prevented from sailing across and passing over the river of the underworld, because, of course, they are not permitted to carry their bones across the dreadful banks and the roaring waters until their bones have rested in their resting places. What Christian heart would incline to these poetic and fabulous inventions, when the Lord Jesus assures us that not a hair of their head will perish, urging Christians not to fear those who, when they have killed the body, have nothing more they can do, so that Christians might die without fear in the hands of enemies who hold their bodies in their power? On this point I spoke enough, as I think, in the first book of The City of God, to blunt the tooth of those who blame the barbarian devastation—especially what Rome recently suffered—on Christian times, and who also throw this objection: that Christ did not come to the aid of his own there. When it is answered to them that the souls of the faithful were received by him according to the merits of their faith, they mock about the unburied corpses. So I explained this whole topic of burial in such words.

problems.quote: so that they may fall securely into the hands of enemies who have their bodies in their power
problems.source_quote: ut inter manus inimicorum, qui eorum corpora in potestate haberent, securi occumberent christiani
problems.why: English inverts the sense: 'securi' modifies Christians, meaning 'without fear/securely,' but 'fall into the hands of enemies' is wrong—'occumberent' means 'fall dead/be slain,' not 'fall into hands.' The clause describes martyrdom (being killed by enemies), not a safe falling into enemy hands.
problems.fix: so that Christians might be slain without fear by enemies who held their bodies in their power

edits.old: so that they may fall securely into the hands of enemies who have their bodies in their power
edits.new: so that Christians might be slain without fear by enemies who held their bodies in their power

fixed: Corrected: 'occumberent' means 'be slain/fall dead,' not 'fall into the hands'; 'securi' modifies the Christians, meaning 'without fear.' The clause describes martyrdom at the hands of enemies who held their bodies in their power.

problems.quote: they are not allowed to be carried across
problems.source_quote: nec ripas datur horrendas et rauca fluenta transportare prius
problems.why: Latin 'datur' with infinitive is impersonal 'it is granted/permitted'; but 'transportare' is active 'to carry across' (the souls carry themselves), not passive 'to be carried across'.
problems.fix: they are not permitted to carry themselves across the dreadful banks and roaring waters

problems.quote: When they are answered that the souls of the faithful were received by him
problems.source_quote: quibus cum responsum fuerit animas fidelium pro suae fidei meritis ab illo fuisse susceptas
problems.why: English 'when they are answered' makes it a temporal clause about the interlocutors, but Latin 'quibus cum responsum fuerit' is dative 'to whom when it has been answered'—the focus is on the response given to them, not their state. Also loses 'pro suae fidei meritis' (according to the merits of their faith).
problems.fix: When it is answered to them that the souls of the faithful were received by him according to the merits of their faith
problems.ruling: Omits 'pro suae fidei meritis' (according to merits of their faith), losing key meaning.

problems.quote: I spoke at length, as far as I think
problems.why: Latin 'satis... sum locutus' means 'I have spoken enough', not 'at length'. 'Satis' = enough/sufficiently, not 'at length'.
problems.fix: I spoke enough, as I think

edits.old: they are not allowed to be carried across
edits.new: they are not permitted to carry themselves across

edits.old: When they are answered that the souls of the faithful were received by him
edits.new: When it is answered to them that the souls of the faithful were received by him according to the merits of their faith

edits.old: I spoke at length, as far as I think
edits.new: I spoke enough, as I think

fixed: Changed 'they are not allowed to be carried across' to 'they are not permitted to carry themselves across': source 'nec ripas datur horrendas et rauca fluenta transportare prius' has impersonal 'datur' with active infinitive 'transportare' (to carry themselves across), not passive.

Changed 'When they are answered that the souls of the faithful were received by him' to 'When it is answered to them that the souls of the faithful were received by him according to the merits of their faith': source 'quibus cum responsum fuerit animas fidelium pro suae fidei meritis ab illo fuisse susceptas' is dative 'to whom when it has been answered', and includes 'pro suae fidei meritis'.
Changed 'I spoke at length, as far as I think' to 'I spoke enough, as I think': source 'satis, quantum existimo, sum locutus' means 'I have spoken enough', not 'at length'.

problems.quote: according to the merits of their faith according to the merits of their faith
problems.why: Phrase duplicated in English, appearing twice where source has it once.
problems.fix: according to the merits of their faith

problems.quote: so that Christians might be slain without fear by enemies who held their bodies in their power
problems.source_quote: ut inter manus inimicorum, qui eorum corpora in potestate haberent, securi occumberent christiani
problems.why: English adds purpose clause 'so that' making enemies' power a means to fearless death; Latin states circumstance, not purpose.
problems.fix: urging Christians not to fear those who, when they have killed the body, have nothing more they can do, even when they fall calmly into the hands of enemies who hold their bodies in their power.
problems.ruling: 'ut...securi occumberent christiani' is purpose: 'so that Christians might lie down slain fearlessly'; English conveys this correctly, not an addition.

problems.why: Latin 'transportare' takes object 'ossa' (bones); English reflexive 'themselves' misrepresents grammar and sense.
problems.ruling: 'transportare' governs 'ossa'; 'carry themselves' wrongly makes unburied persons the object, not their bones.

edits.old: according to the merits of their faith according to the merits of their faith
edits.new: according to the merits of their faith

edits.old: urging Christians not to fear those who, when they have killed the body, have nothing more they can do, so that Christians might be slain without fear by enemies who held their bodies in their power
edits.new: urging Christians not to fear those who, when they have killed the body, have nothing more they can do, even when they fall calmly into the hands of enemies who hold their bodies in their power

edits.old: they are not permitted to carry themselves across
edits.new: they are not permitted to carry their bones across

fixed: Duplicated phrase 'according to the merits of their faith' removed; source has 'pro suae fidei meritis' once.
Purpose clause 'so that' changed to concessive 'even when'; source 'ut inter manus inimicorum... securi occumberent christiani' states circumstance, not purpose.
'carry themselves across' changed to 'carry their bones across'; source 'transportare' takes 'ossa' as object.

fixed.quote: even when they fall calmly into the hands of enemies
fixed.fix: so that Christians might die without fear in the hands of enemies
fixed.note: The 'ut… securi occumberent' purpose clause (so that Christians might die unafraid) was turned into a concession; the proposed fix also repeats text from before the quote.
